comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
This article is pretty narrow. I completely agree that junk like "you're an expert software developer" is a waste of time... but that's not the same as developing skill in using LLMs.

The skills you need these days include:


Understanding the available models and harnesses. These are constantly changing and knowing what's changed and what they can now do that didn't work before remains extremely valuable.

What are the limits of the models you are working with? How likely are they to successfully complete tasks of different difficulty levels?

What tools should you make available to the models, and how? Arming a model with Playwright for browser testing unlocks all sorts of new possibilities, for example

Which programming languages are appropriate for a task? Agents can compile to WebAssembly now, for example - what does that let you build that you couldn't before?

Cost estimates. Something might be possible with an agent at a cost of hundreds of dollars, is that worthwhile?

How can you reduce costs of what you're doing? Telling models to run cheaper subagents for example, which admittedly is one of those tricks that may well become obsolete with future model releases


Honestly though, quite a lot of this comes down to software engineering skills generally. Knowing what's possible on different platforms, how to think about security (what kind of projects need higher security focus), how to break down a large project into smaller segments that are easier to plan and review.

comments.text:
One thing, though: is there any chance I could capture anywhere near $1k/month in value from using these things?


Depends a lot on what you do, and how your employer rewards you. First, there's a very basic sense in which your employer can capture $1k/month pretty trivially. I've had an AI grind through a 4 hour debugging session in minutes (typically in someone else's code), or look at my design and explain to me that I have overlooked a critical constraint buried off in module X, and that I'm about to throw away 6 hours on a dead end. Many such cases, even on my personal open source projects. US FAANG programmers are paid enough that they can earn back a $1k/month AI budget in a couple of days, using $100 of tokens.

In terms of capturing $1k/month for the worker, well, most programmers are paid a salary. So how much of their individual productivity they can translate into promotions, raises, bonuses, etc., depends very heavily on their organizational structure. A lot of places, you may not see any payoff. If you're senior on the tech track, and if you're used to dealing with the people side of things, then sure, maybe you grind out some extra wins at critical moments. Sometimes a good demo at the right moment changes the fate of projects, and LLMs are damn good at demos.

But the larger issue is that, unfortunately, coding agents are getting scary good in a lot of ways. Opus 5.5 is clearly, hands-down, better than any outsourced contractors most organizations can hire. It writes better code, it listens better, it doesn't require people to sit through endless "stakeholder alignment" meetings. You spec the thing, you answer a couple of questions, and a couple of hours later a program pops out. It may not be maintainable, but have you seen the kind of stuff outsourced enterprise contractors often produce? I've been doing this for decades, and outsourced code is pretty terrible. So I expect over the next few years, a lot more programmer layoffs are coming, and no, programmers will not capture tons of value from this technology. It's going raze our industry to the ground. And then, if the AI "labs" can successfully train an AI to do brute-force AI research, it's going to come for even more jobs in 2028.

I am optimistic by what coding models can do, and I am deeply pessimistic about the future of programming—but also the future of many kinds of work.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text:
The core skill in using these tools is the same as the skill you need when writing code by hand. You have to understand the given requirement, the shape of the solution, and how to verify that the code that was produced actually matches the intent. People who don't work with LLMs seem to have this naive idea that it's sort of like a slot machine where you put a query in and then you either get a correct result or some nonsense and you have to try again.

The way this process actually works is that you start by understanding the problem and figuring out how you want to solve it in terms of architecture, data structures, and algorithms that will be used. Then you get the LLM to come up with a rough shape of the solution, and iterate on it until it works the way you want.

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
When I was first learning the C programming language, in my early 20s, it was common knowledge that of the two ways to increment a variable, i++ was slower than ++i. The post-increment function returned the original value of i, which meant stashing a copy of that value before performing the increment. Pre-increment avoided this wasteful operation.

And by “common knowledge” I really mean folklore, because I turned 20 in 1995 and even by then, the most basic of optimising compilers knew to check if you ever used the return value of i++, and if not, skip the operation to save it.


The folklore survives in C++, I think, at least for class-type iterators. With built-in integers and raw pointers the two forms compile to the same thing when the result is discarded. A user-defined postfix operator++(int) has to copy the old value and return it by value, though, while the prefix one increments in place and returns a reference. For trivial iterators like std::vector<T>::iterator an optimizer will usually erase the copy, and with optimization on you probably won't measure much, as this revisit of an old benchmark found. Debug builds are another story, which is why static analyzers like PVS-Studio still flag it++ where the result is unused. ++it costs nothing to type, so it stays my default.

comments.text: The article is about the skill of a human using an LLM, not the markdown files called skills.

comments.author: markerz
comments.text:
I recognize that, but the blog is saying AI skill is mostly people write “common knowledge” into user prompt incantations, system prompts, and SKILL.md files.

My argument is the final “common knowledge” ability AIs really need to fold into their weights is communicating clearly and efficiently.  Everyone triggers this regularly, either through system prompts “Be terse”, skills like caveman, or user prompts like “simpler please” or “write for a new hire”.

comments.author: informal
comments.text:
An AI company can integrate "AI skills" directly into the model, because the capacity of an LLM can be almost infinite technically.

So, "AI skills" will either be too small/niche to be noticed by the AI company, or integrated into the AI models.
